newsitem.title: CHINA: China punishes listed firms in new crackdown.
newsitem.headline: China punishes listed firms in new crackdown.

text.p: China's regulators punished a string of listed firms on Thursday, including China's only domestically listed bank, Shenzhen Development Bank, for speculation and illegal actions in the financial markets.

A central bank statement, carried on state television, signalled the latest crackdown on China's volatile stock markets. It came just a week after regulators ordered state banks to stop trading on the stock markets and wind up their positions in 10 days.

The move against the Shenzhen Development Bank had been expected since the bank earlier this year announced it was carrying out an investigation into share trading malpractices involving its own stock.

The notice from the People's Bank of China, or central bank, and other authorities confirmed the removal of Guangshen Railway Co Ltd's chairman and accountant after it improperly used part of a 300 million yuan investment for share trading.

The statement also ordered the removal of Haitong Securities chairman Li Huiying as well as Kan Zhidong, president of Shenyin & Wanguo Securities and Ma Qingquan, president of China Everbright Securities for illegally obtaining funds from banks.

The securities firms used the funds to speculate in the shares of Shanghai Lujiazui Finance and Trade Zone Development Co Ltd, Shanghai Petrochemical Co Ltd and Shenzhen Nanyou Property Development Co Ltd, it said.

The notice also announced disciplinary action against Shen Ruolei, head of the Shanghai branch of the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China for extending loans to securities houses to trade on the stock market.
The notice also ordered the three securities firms to stop trading for their own account for one year and levied fines on all three.

"(They) created abnormal fluctations in the prices of the these listed companies, upset the normal order of the securities market, hurt the interests of other investors and sparked excessive speculation on the stock market," the notice said.

Referring to the Shenzhen Development Bank, it said it used 311 million yuan from March 1996 to April 1997 to trade illegally in its own stocks and made gains of 90.34 million yuan, violating the commercial bank.

Bank chairman He Yun was dismissed and banned from engaging in financial and securities business for five years. Its illegal earnings would be confiscated and the stocks the bank illegally holds and the proceeds turned over to the state.
"Financial and securities regulators have decided to intensify the crackdown on financial and securities irregularities," the notice said.

They would also crack down on state banks providing capital to other institutions for share speculation, and would dismiss and ban the heads of listed companies, securities companies and big players that used bank loans to trade, it said. They would be prosecuted if the offence was serious.
China's stock markets closed little changed in slow trading due to weak market sentiment with foreign currency B shares slightly higher and domestic A shares falling.
The markets remained under pressure from fears of a new crackdown, with investors reluctant to build positions.

In Shanghai, the B share index rose 0.121 points or 0.16 percent to 82.918 on volume of 15.1 million shares worth $8.9 million. The A index lost 8.252 points or 0.65 percent to 1,265.838 on volume of 268.5 million shares.
In Shenzhen, the B share index rallied 0.96 points or 0.68 percent to close at 143.32 on turnover of HK$73 million.
But the A share index gave up early gains and shed 1.83 points or 0.44 percent to 412.91 with turnover shrinking to 4.8 billion yuan from Wednesday's 7.2 billion.
